Factors Affecting Resistance
1, Length of the Conductor (L)
Resistance is directly proportional to length.
A longer conductor offers more resistance due to increased collisions between electrons and ions.
E.g. A wire twice as long will have twice the resistance.
2. Area of Cross-Section (A)
Resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross- section.
R•— eA thicker conductor has a lower resistance because electrons have more space to flow with fewer collisions.
E.g. A wire with a larger diameter offers less resistance.

3. Temperature (T) eFor metallic conductors, resistance increases with temperature. This happens because atoms vibrate more at higher temperatures, increasing collisions (increase movement of electrons and K.E.).
For semiconductors, resistance decreases with temperature.
Note: The temperature-resistance relationship depends on the material.
4, Nature of the Material (Resistivitt
Different materials have different intrinsic resistivities.
Lower resistivity better conductor (E.g. copper, silver).
Higher resistivity > poorer conductor or insulator (E.g. rubber, plastic).

Materials are classified into:
1. Conductors: Materials that readily allow the flow of electric current, exhibiting igh electrical conductivity and low resistivity. E.g. Copper, silver, gold, aluminum, steel.

2. Semiconductors: Materials with conductivity values between conductors and insulators, offering the possibility to control their conductivity. E.g. Silicon, germanium, and various compounds like arsenide.
3. Insulators: Materials that resist the flow of electric current, having high electrical resistivity and low conductivity.
E.g. Rubber, glass, plastic, air, pure water.

Heating Effect of Electric Current eWhen an electric current flows through a conductor, it produces heat due to the resistance of the conductor. This phenomenon is called the heating effect of electric current.
Heating effect of electric current was given by James Prescott Joule in 1840.
Joule's Law of Heating
The heat produced in a resistor due to the flow of current is given by:
Heat (H) = PRt
Where: H = Heat energy (in joules)
Alternate Forms: I= Current (in amperes)
Using Ohm's Law (V = IR), the formula can also be written as:
R= Resistance (in ohms)
t = Time (in seconds)
Applications of Heating Effect of Electric Current Application Details Electric Heater · Nichrome wire used as heating element Electric bulb Tungsten filament (high melting point)
Electric iron Uses the heating effect to iron clothes Fuse Thin wire with low melting point to protect appliances Important Notes:
